# Depth and Geometry Supervision

Also called: Geometric Regularization, Depth Priors, Geometric Constraints

## Overview
Depth and Geometry Supervision methods accelerate [Neural Radiance Field (NeRF)](#834-neural-radiance-field-nerf.md) optimization and improve geometric accuracy in sparse-view or ill-posed settings by incorporating external or internal geometric priors into the [training loop](#4290-training-loop.md) [S1, 8687-depth-supervised-nerf.md]. Unlike pure photometric approaches that rely solely on color reconstruction, these methods constrain the density field $\sigma$ and rendering weights $w_i$ to align with estimated surface locations, thereby mitigating shape-radiance ambiguity and preventing degenerate solutions such as "floaters" or image-plane collapse [S1, 8687-depth-supervised-nerf.md, 7475-geometric-baseline-regularization.md].

## Shared principles
All methods in this family operate within the augmented loss structure defined by [Regularization and Loss Functions](8586-regularization-and-loss-functions.md), where the [total loss](#4177-total-loss-function.md) $\mathcal{L}_{\text{total}}$ combines the [photometric reconstruction loss](#7799-photometric-reconstruction-loss.md) with geometric [regularization terms](#1413-regularization-losses.md) $\mathcal{L}_{\text{geom}}$ [S1, 7475-geometric-baseline-regularization.md, 8582-regnerf.md]:

$$ \mathcal{L}_{\text{total}} = \mathcal{L}_{\text{photo}} + \lambda_{\text{geom}} \mathcal{L}_{\text{geom}} $$

The geometric term $\mathcal{L}_{\text{geom}}$ typically operates on the rendered expected depth $\hat{D}(\mathbf{r})$ or the ray termination distribution $h(t)$, comparing them against a [depth prior](#7616-depth-regularization.md) $D_{\text{prior}}(\mathbf{r})$ or enforcing internal consistency constraints [S1, 8687-depth-supervised-nerf.md, 9371-depth-structural-consistency-regularization.md]. The rendered expected depth is computed as the weighted average of sample distances:

$$ \hat{D}(\mathbf{r}) = \sum_{i=1}^N w_i t_i $$

where $w_i = T_i (1 - \exp(-\sigma_i \delta_i))$ are the rendering weights and $T_i$ is the accumulated transmittance [S1, 8687-depth-supervised-nerf.md]. Gradients from $\mathcal{L}_{\text{geom}}$ are backpropagated through the [differentiable volume rendering](#43-differentiable-volume-rendering.md) process to update the [NeRF](#1185-nerf-neural-radiance-fields.md) parameters $\theta$ [S1, 8582-regnerf.md]. Common strategies include direct pixel-wise depth matching (MSE/L1), indirect distribution alignment (KL divergence), structural consistency enforcement (KNN/edge preservation), and internal geometric priors (frustum/foreground constraints) [S1, 8687-depth-supervised-nerf.md, 9371-depth-structural-consistency-regularization.md, 7475-geometric-baseline-regularization.md].

## Subtopics

### [Geometric Baseline Regularization](7475-geometric-baseline-regularization.md)
A self-supervised composite loss designed to prevent degenerate solutions (e.g., image-plane collapse) in few-view settings without external depth data. It augments the [photometric loss](#9563-photometric-loss-rawnerf-variant.md) with three internal priors: **Foreground Loss** ($\mathcal{L}_{\text{fg}}$) ensures rays terminate in geometry ($\sum w_i \approx 1$); **Frustum Loss** ($\mathcal{L}_{\text{fr}}$) penalizes density visible in only one view to enforce multi-view consistency; and **Distribution Loss** ($\mathcal{L}_{\text{dist}}$) encourages compact rendering weight distributions along rays. Choose this method when external depth priors are unavailable but geometric plausibility is critical.

### [Guided Optimization of NeRF](7496-guided-optimization-of-nerf.md)
Mitigates shape-radiance ambiguity in indoor scenes by restricting ray sampling to adaptive ranges derived from monocular depth priors. It uses multi-view consistency errors to dynamically adjust near/far sampling bounds ($t_n, t_f$) and refines output depth using confidence scores based on RGB reconstruction errors. Choose this method when monocular depth estimates are available but require refinement to handle scale ambiguity and noise.

### [Single-view NeRF Training with Depth Map](8679-single-view-nerf-training-with-depth-map.md)
Addresses the under-constrained single-panorama reconstruction problem by initializing geometry with estimated depth maps. It explicitly handles scale ambiguity and FOV limitations through a deformable alignment step that jointly optimizes global scale and local bias of perspective depth projections to a canonical panorama depth map. Choose this method for single-view 360-degree scene reconstruction.

### [Depth-Supervised NeRF](8687-depth-supervised-nerf.md)
Accelerates optimization and improves quality in sparse-view settings by incorporating "free" depth priors from SfM keypoints (e.g., COLMAP). It enforces alignment between the rendered ray termination distribution and the probabilistic depth distribution of SfM points using KL divergence, rather than direct pixel-wise matching. Choose this method when sparse 3D keypoints are available from SfM preprocessing.

### [Depth Structural Consistency Regularization](9371-depth-structural-consistency-regularization.md)
Enforces continuity on rendered depth maps using external priors (e.g., DepthAnythingV2) by modeling local depth variations via K-nearest neighbor (KNN) constraints with a boundary tolerance. It preserves sharp structural edges while smoothing noise, distinguishing itself from global [smoothness priors](#11408-smoothness-priors.md). Choose this method when dense, noisy depth priors are available and edge preservation is required.

### [Statistical Depth Refinement](10185-statistical-depth-refinement.md)
A post-processing step that mitigates corrupt stereo depth data (e.g., from specular highlights) by identifying outliers via residual analysis against an underfitting model's smooth depth estimate. It replaces corrupt pixels with statistically smoother alternatives to prevent geometric artifacts. Choose this method when stereo depth inputs contain significant noise or outliers.

### [Novel View Regularization](10806-novel-view-regularization.md)
Mitigates shape-radiance ambiguity in sparse data by injecting synthetic "novel" rays into the optimization loop to provide additional geometric supervision. It renders intermediate viewpoints to reduce overfitting and prevent convergence to local minima with incorrect geometry. Choose this method when training data is extremely sparse and standard regularization fails.

### [3D Point Supervision Loss](12693-3d-point-supervision-loss.md)
Minimizes the Euclidean distance between backprojected rendered depth and ground-truth 3D points in the world coordinate frame. Unlike scalar depth losses, it enforces global geometric connections, enabling robust camera pose registration in sparse-view regimes. Choose this method when 3D point clouds are available and pose refinement is needed.

### Coarse-Fine Consistency Loss
A loss function that enforces consistency between depth estimates of [coarse and fine NeRF](#3406-coarse-to-fine-nerf.md) models to prevent ineffective hierarchical sampling and blur [S1]. It is defined as $L_{cfc} = \mathbb{1}_{\{m_f=1\}} \odot \|z_c - \hat{\nabla}(z_f)\|^2 + \mathbb{1}_{\{m_c=1\}} \odot \|\hat{\nabla}(z_c) - z_f\|^2$, where $z_c$ and $z_f$ are coarse and fine depths, and $m_c/m_f$ are reliability masks determined by reprojection [S1].

### Zero-level set projection
Refines inaccurate median depth from a pre-trained NeRF, particularly at grazing view angles, by iteratively projecting points onto the zero level-set of the surface using TSDF values [S2]. For each 3D point $p$ on the viewing ray, it performs exactly 4 iterative gradient descent steps along the ray direction using the TSDF predicted value to update the point position [S2]. The update is $p_{new} = p_{old} + \alpha \times \hat{t}$, where $[\hat{t}, \hat{n}, \hat{f}] = \phi(p)$ are the tangent, normal, and feature outputs from network $\phi$ evaluated at $p$ [S2]. The parameter $\alpha$ is a small constant controlling the step size [S2]. This is applied in NeRFMeshing as a preprocessing step to initialize mesh geometry before training the SSAN model [S2].

### Robust Depth Loss
A loss function designed to address geometry error degradation in extrapolation performance by being less sensitive to outliers than [L2 loss](#6038-mean-square-error-mse.md), encouraging NeRF to terminate rays around pseudo depth while retaining freedom for inaccurate geometry [S3]. It is defined as:
$$ \mathcal{L}_{\text{robust}}(\mathbf{r}) = \begin{cases} 0.5\Delta D(\mathbf{r})^2, & \text{if } \Delta D(\mathbf{r}) < \beta \\ \beta^2 (0.5 + \log (\frac{\Delta D(\mathbf{r})}{\beta})), & \text{otherwise } \end{cases} $$
where $\Delta D(\mathbf{r}) = \hat{D}(\mathbf{r}) - D(\mathbf{r})$ is the absolute depth difference, $\beta$ is a constant set to 0.1, and $\hat{D}(\mathbf{r})$ is the depth expectation along the camera axis of ray $r(t)$ [S3].

### Depth Supervision with Planar Architectural Depth Priors
Incorporates precomputed depth estimates for floor, ceiling, and walls into NeRF training to enforce geometric constraints on textureless planar surfaces [S4]. It computes depth estimates using semantic segmentation and incorporates these priors into training with MSE and BoundL losses alongside photometric loss [S4]. The BoundL tolerance $\delta$ is set to 1 mm. Loss weights are $\lambda_{\text{color}}=10, \lambda_{\text{depth}}=10$ for a bedroom scene and $\lambda_{\text{color}}=1, \lambda_{\text{depth}}=1$ for a living room scene [S4]. This method converges in 120,000 iterations, faster than photometric-only (200k) or patch-regularization (280k) methods [S4].

### Indirect Depth Supervision (KL Loss)
A [regularization technique](#11314-regularization-techniques.md) that uses depth priors to constrain the NeRF weights by aligning the probability distribution of rendering weights with the depth prior, specifically using KL divergence [S5]. The loss is $L_{KL} = \sum_{i}^{N_r} \sum_{t=t_n}^{t_f} D(r_i) - \epsilon \log w_k \exp(-\frac{(t - D(r_i))^2}{2\hat{\sigma}^2}) \Delta t_k$, where $w_k$ are rendering weights, $t_k$ are sampled points, $\Delta t_k$ are distances, $D(r_i)$ is ground truth depth, $\epsilon$ is a kernel parameter, and $\hat{\sigma}$ is a variance parameter [S5]. The URF loss is another form of indirect supervision, but KL loss is selected as the representative due to URF's lack of open-source implementation [S5].

### Geometry and Opacity Regularization
Includes [sparsity loss](#1203-nerf-training-configuration.md) $L_S = \frac{1}{N} \sum_{i=1}^{N} O(i)$ to encourage sparse opacity and suppress floaters, and opacity loss $L_O = -\frac{1}{N} \sum_{i=1}^{N} [O(i) \cdot \log(O(i)) + (1 - O(i)) \cdot \log(1 - O(i))]$ to encourage opacity values to be 0 or 1, avoiding translucent effects [S6].

### Depth Filtering with RGB Confidence
Filters predicted depth maps by computing a per-pixel confidence metric based on the reconstruction error between predicted and ground truth RGB images [S7, unofficial]. The confidence map is computed as $1$ minus the mean absolute error between normalized predicted and ground truth RGBs across channels [S7, unofficial]. This is used in parallel processing pools to filter depth outputs [S7, unofficial].

### Direct Depth Supervision
A training objective that directly compares the depth rendered by the NeRF with a ground truth depth prior using a pixel-wise loss function, including MSE ($L_{MSE} = \sum ||D(r_i) - \hat{D}(r_i)||^2$) and L1 ($L_{L1} = \sum |D(r_i) - \hat{D}(r_i)|$) [S5].

### GeoAug
An approach that uses data augmentation by rendering new training images with new noisy camera poses using DSNeRF as a baseline and using depth as regularization [S8].

## Background
Depth and geometry supervision in NeRFs originated from the observation that photometric loss alone is insufficient for recovering accurate geometry, especially in sparse-view or textureless scenarios [S1, 8687-depth-supervised-nerf.md]. Early work by [DS-NeRF](8687-depth-supervised-nerf.md) demonstrated that leveraging sparse 3D keypoints from Structure-from-Motion (SfM) pipelines could significantly accelerate convergence and improve geometric fidelity [S1, S2][S3]. Subsequent research expanded to include dense depth priors from monocular estimators [S1, 9371-depth-structural-consistency-regularization.md], stereo matching [S1, 10185-statistical-depth-refinement.md], and self-supervised geometric constraints [S1, 7475-geometric-baseline-regularization.md]. These methods are widely used in applications requiring high-fidelity 3D reconstruction from limited views, such as robotics, augmented reality, and cultural heritage digitization [S1, S4, S8].
